summary.headline: Yes for serving, search, audio and classical ML; not yet for training research or pure-Rust image generation.
summary.summary: Rust is right when the model is already trained and the job is to serve it, search with it, or ship it inside a product as a single binary. LLM inference, embeddings, vector and full-text search, speech, OCR, Arrow data work and classical ML all have maintained Rust cores, and several apps build directly on them. It is wrong for training research, maintained experiment tracking, pure-Rust image generation and some video encode paths, where Python still leads or Rust tools are thin. Use Rust for the runtime and keep Python for data prep, evaluation and model export.

jobs.verdict: Rust engines cover GGUF and quantized models, OpenAI-compatible serving and ONNX, and [[burn]] and [[candle]] keep the work in Rust. Limits: vendor GPU toolchains, narrow model coverage on young servers, and wrappers such as [[ort]] that pull in C++.

[[rig]], [[swiftide]] and [[rmcp]] cover agents, RAG, tools and MCP, and typed clients exist for major APIs. Evaluation and regression testing exists in [[rig]], [[adk-rust]] and [[awaken]] but is fragmented, so teams still glue harnesses.

[[burn]], [[candle]] and [[boostr]] train and fine-tune on a single machine; [[nexar]] spans nodes over QUIC. Experiment logging exists through [[tboard-rs]], but it is unmaintained, and sweeps and comparison dashboards are still thin.

ASR, TTS, VAD, diarization and audio decode all have Rust options, with [[parakeet-rs]], [[any-tts]] and [[earshot]] doing the work in Rust. The strongest engines still sit on ONNX Runtime or libtorch underneath.

Tokenizers, embeddings, vector stores and full-text search are solid Rust cores other Rust apps run on: [[tokenizers]], [[fastembed-rs]], [[qdrant]], [[lancedb]], [[tantivy]]. Reranking models are fewer and NER still leans on wrappers.

Decode, transform, detect and OCR are covered by [[kornia-rs]], [[imageproc]] and [[aha]]. Detection often runs through [[inference]] or [[usls]] over ONNX Runtime; generation exists through native-backed [[diffusion-rs]], with no maintained Rust-native diffusion.

[[vidr]] decodes and restores on GPU or CPU and encodes H.264, HEVC and AV1 via NVENC or Vulkan Video; [[containr]] handles MP4/MKV. CPU HEVC encode, CPU H.264 above Baseline, VA-API, AMD/Intel Vulkan Video and maintained tracking remain limits; [[similari]] is unmaintained.
Pure-Rust PDF parsing and OCR exist: [[edgeparse]], [[pdf-oxide]], [[ocrs]], [[franken-ocr]]. Layout and table models usually mean [[docling]] or [[oar-ocr]], which wrap ONNX Runtime or PDFium.
[[linfa]], [[smartcore]] and [[perpetual]] cover regression, clustering, SVM and boosting, with [[augurs]] for time series. Feature depth is below scikit-learn and tuning tools are thin.

Arrays, linear algebra, FFT, statistics, optimisation and ODEs are met in pure Rust: [[ndarray]], [[nalgebra]], [[faer]], [[rustfft]], [[statrs]], [[argmin]]. Sparse solvers and GPU FFT are the weak spots.

[[burn]] and [[cubecl]] give portable kernels across CUDA, Metal, Vulkan and WebGPU with autodiff and attention; [[candle]] and [[numr]] add leaner paths. Backend coverage varies and WebGPU is often single precision only.

Arrow, Parquet, Safetensors, GGUF, Zarr, HDF5 and NumPy files read and write in Rust: [[arrow-rs]], [[polars]], [[safetensors]], [[zarrs]], [[hdf5-pure]]. Streaming into a training loop still needs glue you write.

use_now.use_for: Local LLM and multimodal serving behind an OpenAI-compatible API
use_now.why: Rust engine and SDK for text, vision, speech and embeddings, GGUF quantized models, tool calling and an MCP client; the default build needs no C compiler.

use_now.use_for: Training and inference framework with many GPU backends
use_now.why: Tensors, autodiff, ONNX import and CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, WebGPU and CPU backends written in Rust; several apps and servers here build on it.

use_now.use_for: Minimal Rust framework for custom model inference
use_now.why: Small Rust-first tensor library with CUDA and Metal, GGUF and safetensors support; engines such as [[candle-vllm]] and [[cake]] are built on top.

use_now.use_for: Agents, RAG, tools and MCP inside a Rust service
use_now.why: A single library for providers, tool calling, vector stores, streaming and OpenTelemetry, with session stores and an MCP client already written.

use_now.use_for: MCP servers and clients in Rust
use_now.why: Official Rust MCP SDK with tools, resources, prompts, OAuth, tasks and stdio or Streamable HTTP transports; maintained and widely depended on.

use_now.use_for: Calling OpenAI and compatible APIs from Rust
use_now.why: Covers streaming, batches, embeddings, files and vector stores with retries and WASM support, and handles OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

use_now.use_for: Embedding full-text search in your own service
use_now.why: Rust search library with BM25, facets, fast fields and mmap indexes; other catalogue servers run on the same engine.

use_now.use_for: Self-hosted vector search at production scale
use_now.why: Rust vector database with dense, sparse and multi-vector search, filtering, hybrid fusion and sharding; the Rust client talks to it directly.

use_now.use_for: DataFrames and large-table cleanup in Rust
use_now.why: Arrow-based query engine with lazy plans and larger-than-memory streaming, usable from Rust with no Python process.

use_now.use_for: Arrow and Parquet IO under your own data code
use_now.why: The official Rust Arrow implementation with IPC, CSV, Parquet and Flight protocol work, and the layer [[datafusion]] and [[polars]] read through.

use_now.use_for: Speech to text and diarization on your own machine
use_now.why: Parakeet ASR and diarization over ONNX Runtime or a pure-Rust [[burn]] backend, including streaming and multitalker models.

use_now.use_for: Static embeddings generated in pure Rust
use_now.why: Loads static embedding models from Hugging Face or local paths, with quantized safetensors and no native runtime.

watch.use_for: Ahead-of-time ONNX compilation for embedded and bare metal
watch.why: Turns ONNX graphs into plain Rust with no runtime, with ASR, VAD, TTS and OCR examples. Young, no loop support and only partial Einsum.

watch.use_for: NumPy-role tensors on CPU, CUDA and WebGPU
watch.why: Pure-Rust kernels with no cuBLAS or MKL, plus autograd and FFT. Not a deep-learning framework: no attention, quantization or ROCm.
Trains from CSV or Parquet over SIMD, WGPU and CUDA paths. No XGBoost or ONNX export yet and little outside use.

watch.use_for: Pure-Rust CPU OCR for documents, tables and charts
watch.why: Hand-ported document OCR as a single binary with no GPU or FFI. Only runs its named models; it is not a generic runtime.

watch.use_for: GPU video decode, model run and AV1 encode
watch.why: NVDEC, NVENC and Vulkan Video with frames as tensors. Missing VA-API, AMD and Intel Vulkan Video, CPU HEVC encode, CPU H.264 above Baseline and fragmented MP4 input.

watch.use_for: Agent loop with several wire protocols, native or wasm
watch.why: Streams, runs tools and keeps JSONL sessions, and deploys to Cloudflare Workers. No vector store or task-graph orchestration.

build_today.goal: Private document Q&A service that runs on your own hardware
build_today.why: Embeddings, vector search, retrieval and generation all run as Rust services, so the runtime needs no Python.
build_today.watch_out: Retrieval quality is on you; build a regression harness and check answers against real documents before launch.

build_today.goal: Self-hosted chat API that also serves your own Burn model
build_today.why: A single OpenAI-compatible front end for a GGUF LLM and a custom Burn or ONNX model, all written in Rust.
build_today.watch_out: [[furnace]] has almost no GPU measurements and API churn; pin versions and load-test it first.

build_today.goal: Meeting transcription app with speaker labels and search
build_today.why: Voice activity, ASR, diarization and audio decode run locally, and [[minutes]] already wires them into a searchable store.
build_today.watch_out: Diarization is capped at a small speaker count on some paths, and GPU builds pull ONNX Runtime natives in.

build_today.goal: Churn or risk model trained and served from Rust
build_today.why: Preprocessing, boosting and explainability work in pure Rust, reading CSV or Parquet directly.
build_today.watch_out: There is no scikit-learn breadth and no maintained tracker; you write cross-validation and comparison yourself.

build_today.goal: Full-text and semantic search over a PDF corpus
build_today.why: PDF to structured text, BM25 indexing, local embeddings and a vector store, all with Rust cores.
build_today.watch_out: [[edgeparse]] is young and table extraction is heuristic; measure recall on your own documents.

holes_filled.hole: Local LLM inference with OpenAI-compatible serving
holes_filled.note: A team can ship an internal model endpoint as a Rust binary. Checkpoint conversion can be done in Rust too, though some model exports still use Python tooling.
Rust services expose and consume tools over MCP directly, with typed schemas and OAuth, so no Python bridge is needed.

holes_filled.hole: Dense, sparse and lexical retrieval in Rust
holes_filled.note: All retrieval modes run as Rust cores; the Python SDK is a client choice rather than a runtime dependency.

holes_filled.hole: Speech to text, voice activity and diarization on your own hardware
holes_filled.note: On-device transcription ships today. The cost is native ONNX Runtime or libtorch builds on GPU paths.

holes_filled.hole: Arrow, Parquet, Safetensors and GGUF file work
holes_filled.note: Dataset and weight IO no longer forces a Python step, and the same crates back bigger engines in this catalogue.

holes_filled.hole: Classical ML and gradient boosting on tables
holes_filled.note: Tabular models train and serve in Rust. Scikit-learn parity is not there for the long tail of estimators.

holes_filled.hole: Pure-Rust ONNX inference without the C++ runtime
holes_filled.note: [[tract]] and [[oxionnx]] run exported models without ONNX Runtime in the build. [[lele]] compiles fixed graphs only, with no Loop and partial Einsum, so check operators per model.

holes_open.hole: Maintained experiment tracking, sweeps and comparison dashboards for Rust training
holes_open.impact: Stops research teams from replacing Python for training; losses, configs and runs end up in a separate system.
holes_open.workaround: [[tboard-rs]] writes TensorBoard files but is unmaintained; otherwise log to an external tracker over HTTP or keep training in Python.

holes_open.hole: Unified release-gating evaluation and regression suites for LLM applications
holes_open.impact: Teams must stitch evals from [[adk-rust]], [[awaken]] and [[rig]] before they can gate an agent release on measured quality.
holes_open.workaround: Use [[rig]] replay plus [[opentelemetry-langfuse]] traces, or keep a Python eval suite.

holes_open.hole: Rust-native text-to-image generation without a wrapped diffusion engine
holes_open.impact: Product teams that need generated images must accept a native dependency or leave Rust for the feature.
holes_open.workaround: Use [[diffusion-rs]] over stable-diffusion.cpp, or a Python service; [[diffusers-rs]] is an unmaintained Torch port.

holes_open.hole: Hardware video paths beyond NVDEC/NVENC and Vulkan Video, plus CPU HEVC/H.264 encode
holes_open.impact: Media teams needing AMD or Intel hardware encode, CPU HEVC, or CPU H.264 beyond Baseline must stay on ffmpeg bindings or another language.
holes_open.workaround: Use [[vidr]] NVENC/Vulkan Video paths or [[rav1r]] for AV1; shell out to ffmpeg for the missing CPU and AMD/Intel paths.

holes_open.hole: Maintained general multi-object tracking across video frames
holes_open.impact: Video analytics teams must build tracking around detections or accept an unmaintained library.
holes_open.workaround: Use tracking in [[inference]] or write a tracker over detections; [[similari]] has SORT variants but is unmaintained.

charts.takeaway: Rust ML work often blends pure Rust with wrapped native engines or build tools, so build portability and native dependency risk need early review.
GPU support is fragmented and often undocumented, so teams should verify backend coverage for their target hardware before choosing the stack.
Release activity is uneven across the ecosystem, making freshness and maintenance cadence essential checks rather than assumed signs of maturity.
